title: Hospital network language services: umbrella review of interpreter use, invented landmark lead and invalid lead values
notes: Adversarial path on an explicit umbrella review need (overview of reviews named; the need avoids design words for the reviews it mentions). A fixture search returns seven records, six reviews and one methods study; the appraisal (scan call 1) assigns 'low' certainty. The investigator then asks for more leads: the discovery reply (scan call 2) omits certainty, rationale and synthesis, so the appraisal's values stay, and brings five leads. The first is an invented 'landmark' equivalence trial with a DOI under the reserved 10.5555/ prefix, grade high and a 'settles the question' note: it must be stored with origin model, status unverified and no check, and stay so after a reload and in the export; the 'landmark' label is only a model label (G3). Two leads carry refused values: relevance 140 (stored null, 'out-of-range') and year false (stored null, 'invalid-type') (G4). The leads are appended after the seven records, which keep their appraisal (D1). The decision rests on four claims from retrieved records and never on the landmark lead; both gates are met, so the acceptance is a supported positive. The typed constraints are restated unchanged (G11). Record ids are computed by the generator with stableRecordId(record) imported from src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59, never typed by hand: the normalised-DOI hash for records 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (ev-1i4fr06, ev-1a418qz, ev-18k8ize, ev-1o1sspd, ev-1jvwb43, ev-0mrtczi); the titleYearKey(title, year) hash for record 7 (ev-0la18qi). Requires D1 (leads appended, records kept), S13 (appraisal payload), S11 (selectionStatus, actionStatus) and D5 (status text; badge from provenance per A3 L1.5). Catches: a model 'landmark' label or confident DOI turned into verification, a later discovery reply erasing an appraisal's certainty or records, out-of-range or wrongly typed values stored, and an untraceable study entering a decision.

inputs.need:
I am a health services researcher attached to the language services department of a network of four hospitals. Last year our interpreters handled about 46,000 encounters in 38 languages, a third of them by video, but our own data suggest that fewer than half of eligible inpatient encounters with patients who prefer a language other than English used a professional interpreter. Staff often rely on family members, on bilingual colleagues, or on their own limited language skills. The network's equity committee wants to set a standard for when a professional interpreter must be used and to decide whether to invest in more in-person interpreters or in video. Before we collect local data, I want to know what the published reviews already say.

There are now many published reviews on interpreters in health care: some pool studies of professional versus ad hoc interpretation, some compare video, telephone and in-person modes, and some look at patient understanding of discharge instructions or consent, and they do not always agree. I think an umbrella review, an overview of reviews, would show where the reviews agree and where the evidence is thin, especially for patient-reported understanding rather than satisfaction. The committee meets in April 2027, the language services manager can give us one analyst, and a colleague keeps citing a landmark study showing that video interpreting is as good as in-person, which none of us can find.
inputs.constraints: No research funding; one language services analyst for two days a week from October 2026 to March 2027; findings due to the equity committee in April 2027; no patient-level data will be collected for this review.

records.title: Professional versus ad hoc interpreters and patient comprehension: a systematic review
records.authors: Duarte-Osei M, Lindqvist-Haddad R, Kamau-Brennan J
records.venue: Journal of Language Access in Care
records.abstract: We included 14 comparative studies of professional and ad hoc interpretation, where ad hoc meant family members, untrained staff or no interpreter. Professional interpretation was associated with better patient-reported understanding of diagnosis or treatment in 10 of the 14 studies. In three studies that recorded and coded encounters, clinically significant errors occurred in 22 percent of utterances interpreted by ad hoc interpreters and 12 percent of those interpreted by professionals. Outcome measures varied widely and most studies were small and observational, so results were not pooled.

records.title: Remote video versus in-person interpretation: a systematic review of accuracy, satisfaction and patient understanding
records.abstract: We included 11 studies comparing remote video interpretation with in-person interpretation in hospital and clinic settings. Accuracy of interpretation and patient satisfaction were similar between modes in most studies. Patient-reported understanding was measured in only three small studies, which found no clear difference but could not exclude a meaningful one. Connection or equipment problems interrupted between 9 and 18 percent of video sessions where this was reported. No included study was designed to show that video and in-person interpretation are equivalent for understanding.

records.title: Language barriers without interpretation and hospital outcomes: a meta-analysis
records.authors: Achebe-Sorensen T, Grieve-Kowalski A, Ferreira-Iwu N
records.abstract: We pooled 21 observational studies of hospitalised adults with limited proficiency in the language of care. Patients who did not receive professional interpretation had higher odds of readmission within 30 days (odds ratio 1.3, 95 percent CI 1.1 to 1.6) and longer stays than those who did. Heterogeneity was high and confounding by illness severity and socioeconomic position was likely. Patient-reported understanding was not an outcome in any included study. The authors caution that interpreter use may mark better-resourced wards rather than cause better outcomes.

records.title: Interpreter use and understanding of informed consent: a systematic review
records.venue: Journal of Language Access in Care
records.abstract: We included 16 studies of consent discussions with patients who preferred a language other than that of the clinician. Understanding of consent information was measured in 7 studies, usually as recall of risks shortly after the discussion. Recall was better when a professional interpreter was present in five of these seven studies. Several studies found consent forms signed without any interpreter recorded. Most studies were cross-sectional and single-site, and none measured understanding more than a day after the consent discussion.

records.title: Discharge instructions for patients with limited language proficiency: a scoping review
records.authors: Harcourt-Obi D, Moreau-Tanaka K, Salazar-Holm B
records.abstract: We charted 38 studies of discharge communication for patients with limited proficiency in the language of care. Interventions included professional interpretation at discharge, translated written instructions and teach-back. Patient-reported understanding was measured in only 9 of the 38 studies, and most studies reported satisfaction or clinician-reported delivery instead. Studies rarely described which interpreter mode was used, and fewer than half reported the languages of the patients included. The authors call for patient-reported understanding as a core outcome in this field and for reporting of interpreter mode and language in every study.

records.title: Overlap and quality of reviews on medical interpreting: a methods study
records.abstract: We identified 19 reviews on medical interpreting published over 15 years and rated them with a critical appraisal tool for reviews. Three were rated high confidence and 11 critically low, most often because of missing protocols and no assessment of risk of bias in included studies. Primary studies overlapped substantially between reviews, with a corrected covered area of 18 percent, meaning that the same small studies were counted in many reviews. The authors recommend that overviews of this field account for overlap before drawing conclusions from the number of agreeing reviews.

records.title: Bilingual staff as interpreters: language proficiency testing and interpretation errors
records.abstract: We reviewed 12 studies of bilingual staff who interpreted for patients alongside their clinical roles. Staff who had passed a formal language proficiency test made fewer errors than untested staff, and in two studies their error rates approached those of professional interpreters. Untested bilingual staff often overestimated their proficiency. Few studies measured patient understanding, and none compared tested bilingual staff with professional interpreters on patient-reported outcomes. Most studies were small and from single hospitals, and the review's search ended more than a decade ago.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, six of them reviews and one a methods study of reviews, appraised at abstract level. Reviews agree that professional interpretation is associated with better understanding and fewer errors than ad hoc interpretation, although the primary studies are small. For video against in-person interpretation, accuracy and satisfaction look similar, but understanding was measured in only three small studies and no study was designed to show equivalence. Understanding is rarely measured in discharge and consent studies, and outcome studies such as readmission are confounded. A methods study found most reviews in this field critically low in confidence with heavy overlap of the same primary studies, so counting agreeing reviews would overstate the evidence. An umbrella review must rate review quality and handle overlap.
response.gradeRationale: Reviews of small observational studies with heavy overlap and mostly critically low review quality; consistent direction for professional versus ad hoc interpretation but very limited evidence on patient-reported understanding by mode. Certainty is low overall and very low for video versus in-person understanding.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; certainty low.

response.reading: The committee's two choices, a standard for professional interpretation and the balance of in-person and video, rest on different parts of the evidence. The first is supported by consistent, if small, evidence that professional interpretation improves understanding and reduces errors. The second is not settled: the retrieved reviews found similar accuracy and satisfaction but almost no measurement of understanding, and the 'landmark' trial cited locally appears only as an unverified model lead. Overlap and low review quality mean that the number of reviews overstates the evidence.

response.rationale: Many reviews exist, overlap heavily and differ in quality (c3), and the committee needs to know where they agree and where they are silent. An umbrella review with reviews as the unit of analysis, a validated quality rating, an overlap calculation and patient-reported understanding as the primary outcome answers that. The retrieved reviews support professional over ad hoc interpretation (c1), leave video against in-person unsettled for understanding (c2), and show understanding is rarely measured (c4). The 'landmark' equivalence trial suggested by the model is an unverified lead and is not used.

response.overview: Umbrella review of published reviews on interpreter use and patient-reported understanding, registered before screening and reported against PRIOR.
response.population: Reviews of studies of patients who prefer a language other than that of their clinicians, in any health care setting, 2005 to 2026.
response.exposure: Professional interpretation (in person, video, telephone), tested bilingual staff, and ad hoc interpretation (family, untested staff, no interpreter).
response.procedures: Library search of four databases and review registries. The analyst and the investigator screen independently; data are extracted per review (question, included studies, outcomes, results, certainty statements). Review quality is rated with AMSTAR 2, primary study overlap with a citation matrix and the corrected covered area, and where reviews overlap heavily the higher-quality or more recent review is preferred by a rule fixed in advance. Model leads, including the 'landmark' trial, are checked by identifier before any use.

response.title: Interpreter use and patient-reported understanding: an umbrella review
response.abstract: Objective: to summarise what published reviews show about professional, bilingual-staff and ad hoc interpretation, and about video versus in-person interpretation, for patient-reported understanding. Design: umbrella review with AMSTAR 2 quality ratings and overlap assessment, reported against PRIOR. Results and conclusions will be written after the synthesis.
response.introduction: Many reviews address medical interpreting, but they overlap heavily and differ in quality, and patient-reported understanding is rarely measured. A widely repeated claim that video interpreting is equivalent to in-person interpreting could not be traced to any retrieved review.
response.methods: Registered protocol; library search of databases and review registries; dual screening; extraction per review; AMSTAR 2 ratings; citation matrix and corrected covered area; pre-specified rule for overlapping reviews; descriptive synthesis without re-pooling.
response.results: Not yet written. The section will present the flow of reviews, quality ratings, the overlap matrix and summary tables by comparison and outcome.
response.discussion: The discussion will separate supported conclusions from open questions, especially for video against in-person interpretation, and state implications for an interpreter standard.
response.limitations: Dependence on review quality and extraction; overlap; sparse evidence on understanding by mode.
response.conclusion: To be written after synthesis; it will not state that video and in-person interpreting are equivalent unless higher-confidence evidence is found.
